newsitem.title: NORWAY: U.S. cautious as NATO gathers on Bosnia.
newsitem.headline: U.S. cautious as NATO gathers on Bosnia.

text.p: NATO defence ministers gathered on Tuesday for a two-day meeting that will focus on continued peacekeeping in Bosnia next year and the alliance's eastward expansion, which is firmly opposed by Russia.

The informal talks, starting on Wednesday, will give the 16 ministers their first chance after the Bosnian elections to discuss a possible follow-on force to be sent to the war-torn country after the current mission's mandate ends in December.

But U.S. Defence secretary William Perry, arriving for the meeting, continued to voice American caution over predictions by German Defence Minister Volker Ruehe and others that a NATO-led peace implementation force (IFOR) of over 50,000 troops will be replaced after it is withdrawn this December. .

"In the last analysis, they (other countries) will reserve their final judgment until they see what the requests are," Perry said. "I don't think we (the United States) can have a position until we see what the request is, what the mission is, what the force structure requested is."

The ministers will also be able to meet new Russian Defence Minister Igor Rodionov, who on Thursday will sign an agreement with Perry and Norwegian Defence Minister Joergen Kosmo on tackling Russian military pollution in the Arctic.
Officials said Bosnia was first on the agenda in the talks in a tightly guarded hotel in the picturesque coastal town of Bergen.

Many western allies accept that a force will have to stay to prevent conflict and give last year's Dayton peace accords time to take root, but its size, make-up and mandate have yet to be agreed. The issue is sensitive in the United States where presidential elections take place on November 5.

President Bill Clinton has promised that 15,000 U.S. troops will not stay in Bosnia beyond the current IFOR mandate, which ends on December 20. But America's main European allies have made clear they will not stay without a U.S. troop commitment.
NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana has said the alliance will have to remain engaged beyond the end of the year, probably with a smaller force including U.S. troops.

Elections on September 14 underlined Bosnia's ethnic divide and highlighted the problems in trying to create the common institutions foreseen in Dayton to unify the country. Even with a big NATO security operation, few refugees took the risk of crossing ethnic boundaries to vote in their former homes.
Former Warsaw Pact states, such as Poland and Hungary, want to remain and see close cooperation in the new force as a way of strengthening their case for NATO membership next year.
NATO's expansion, a touchy issue for the Russians, will be discussed on Thursday morning before the ministers go into a so-called 16+1 meeting with Rodionov, officials said.

Earlier on Tuesday, NATO defence ministers meeting ex-Warsaw Pact and non-aligned officials in Copenhagen sought to encourage the former Soviet Baltic republics in their bid for membership while reassuring Russia that an enlarged alliance was no threat.
In a speech prepared for delivery to a closed-door seminar on Baltic Sea regional security, Ruehe said eastern European countries not immediately able to join NATO must not feel rejected.
"Neither NATO nor the European Union can take in all countries who wish to become members at the same time. But the door will remain open to those who cannot join with the first wave," he said.
Although a firm decision on new members is not expected before a NATO summit early next year, Hungary, Poland and the Czech Republic are widely seen as the most immediate candidates.
